summary: We developed Jezero Pathfinder, a browser-based tool for planning safe astronaut walks (EVAs) in Jezero Crater, Perseverance’s landing site. It layers real NASA CTX imagery, a 20 m USGS elevation model and a slope map we made in QGIS into one map where users place waypoints and plan a route. Each route is safety-checked automatically: slope, walk vs. rover legs, suit consumables, walk-back distance, radiation dose and the daylight EVA window, giving every leg a GO, Caution or No-go. A first-person Helmet HUD then shows the plan through the astronaut’s eyes. The first humans on Mars will have no paths and little margin for error; Pathfinder turns real planetary data into a safe, explainable plan.
details:
Jezero Pathfinder: Astronaut Route & Exploration System

What it does and how it works
Jezero Pathfinder is a single-page web tool for planning, checking and walking a human EVA (spacewalk on the surface) inside Jezero Crater on Mars, where Perseverance landed. A mission planner places waypoints on a map of the crater. The tool works out each leg’s distance, bearing, slope, travel time and status. The map has three layers of the same EVA area. The optical layer is the MRO Context Camera (CTX) mosaic. The elevation layer is the 20 m CTX DEM (a terrain height map). The slope layer we derived from that DEM in QGIS. Users can also turn route and hazard layers on and off, change overlay opacity, draw on the map, and zoom between the whole crater and the EVA area.

Every leg goes through an automatic safety check:

  • Slope bands: 0–15% is GO, 15–30% is Caution, and over 30% is No-go.
  • Walking legs: up to 2 km at 2 km/h, with the EV1 + EV2 buddy system.
  • Rover: a pressurised rover at 8 km/h takes over automatically once a leg is too long to walk.
  • Walk-back limit: the crew must always be able to walk home.
  • Suit time: 8 hours of suit consumables plus a reserve, inside a 09:00–15:00 local solar time EVA window.

The tool also estimates radiation dose using MSL RAD surface data (dose rate × EVA time). A solar particle event simulator shows how quickly the crew would have to get back to the habitat or rover. Once the plan passes, it goes to a helmet HUD view. The HUD shows the current leg and its GO status, a heading tape, the slope against its limit, the next waypoint, life-support margin, walk-back distance and dose. ARES, a built-in voice or typed assistant, takes commands during the walk. All the planning limits can be changed in a settings panel.

Our sample EVA visits Octavia E. Butler Landing, Delta Approach, Enchanted Lake and Hawksbill Gap. It covers 6.10 km in 3 h 36 m over four legs, all GO. That leaves 4 h 24 m of suit time spare, with an estimated crew dose of 0.096 mSv.

Benefits

  • Terrain, safety rules, life support and radiation are checked together in one place, not across separate datasets.
  • Planners see straight away why a leg is GO or no-go.
  • The same plan becomes the astronaut’s in-helmet guidance, so the plan and what the crew does stay the same.
  • Because every limit can be edited, it works for other crews, suits, rovers or landing sites.

Intended impact
We want to show how open NASA and USGS orbital data can support real decisions about crew safety on future human missions to Mars. Jezero’s ancient river delta is one of the best places to look for signs of past habitability. Our tool helps plan how astronauts could safely reach and sample it. It is also a learning tool: students and the public can see how terrain, distance, time and radiation limit what explorers can do on Mars.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single-page web app [add the mapping library you used, e.g. Leaflet or OpenLayers, plus anything for the voice assistant]
  • Analysis software: QGIS for slope analysis and data preparation
  • Data: USGS Mars 2020 CTX DEM mosaic (20 m), NASA PDS MRO CTX imagery, NASA/JPL Jezero geology, MSL RAD surface radiation (Hassler et al. 2014), CRISM carbonate data, Perseverance raw images, the NASA/USGS Viking Orbiter mosaic, and JPL Mars Trek
  • Hosting: GitHub (github.com/Ebz142/ARES_Mars_-Exploration)
  • Hardware: none beyond standard laptops; it runs in any web browser

How it is creative
Most Mars map viewers only display data. Jezero Pathfinder turns that data into a decision: each leg gets a clear GO, Caution or No-go. It covers the whole EVA, from planning through the safety check to the astronaut’s-eye HUD. The radiation dose and solar storm simulator add a time-based risk that a static map can’t show.

Factors we considered

  • Crew safety comes first: slope limits, the buddy system, walk-back distance, suit consumables plus a reserve, and radiation exposure.
  • Realistic movement speeds, and the switch from walking to the rover.
  • The Mars environment: about 6–9 hPa air pressure, −80 to −20 °C temperature swings, and daylight-only EVA windows.
  • Scientific value: the route goes to the delta deposits where carbonate- and clay-bearing rocks are found.
  • Data quality and honesty: we only use open NASA and USGS sources, and we state that no evidence of life has been found.
  • Ease of use: one page that runs in a browser, with a clear colour-coded status.
